concept: definition and origin in randomized trials
outcome_text: Randomized allocation is the design that makes causal comparison possible and is the basis for the Cookie Cats experiment.
gate_30 is the control and gate_40 is the treatment; retention is measured by arm.
The primary metric is 7-day retention at 19.02% vs 18.20%.
CTR in the Upworthy archive is clicks divided by impressions, which is a probability-like conversion metric for each arm.
The null is no difference in D7 retention; the alternative is a difference between arms.
The decision threshold is alpha=0.05 two-sided.
Power is set to 0.80, so beta=0.20.
Power is 80% at the pre-specified MDE and sample size.
The decision MDE is 1.0 pp absolute lift on D7 retention.
Required sample size at 1.0 pp lift is roughly 38,854 users per arm for D1 and 24,259 per arm for D7.
The analysis uses 14-day game-rounds and a 7-day retention outcome, so duration is built into the metric choice.
No timestamp data means we cannot separate novelty effects, weekday effects, and traffic mix changes.
There are zero nulls and zero duplicate user IDs in the Cookie Cats data.
SRM chi-square p-value is 0.0086, which is a flag under the standard threshold of 0.05.
The D7 retention test uses a two-proportion z-test with pooled p-value.
D7 retention CI is about [-1.33, -0.31] pp for the difference.
The absolute lift is -0.82 pp for D7 retention.
The effect is statistically significant but below the decision MDE, so it is not worth shipping.
There are no timestamps, so peeking and early stopping cannot be audited from the raw file.
Holm adjustment keeps the D7 result significant while the D1 result is not.
Subgroup analysis changed direction after conditioning on rounds >= 40; this is a selection-bias warning, not proof of treatment benefit.
Most players never reached the gate, which dilutes the observed exposure effect.
Exposure differs by arm in the rounds >= 40 subgroup, and the effect is interpreted as exploratory.
The recommendation is to not ship gate_40 on retention evidence.
Low traffic, weak instrumentation, or impossible measurement make causal tests less useful; this repo documents those limits in the playbook.
